content:
David Kinkead said:

Recent Quanta article that I'm not sure I've seen posted here yet.

Thanks for posting!

My first reaction: For the sake of diversity, can we please have both? Doodling with chalk on a blackboard, dreaming up maths while walking through the woods, ambiguity, explaining ideas with pictures, an emphasis on beauty, and the soft side of maths, yin.
But also, rigour, precision, formalize in ITPs, abstracting, codification, fussing about every tiny detail, and at the same time the large meta structure of maths, the hard side of maths, yang.

I feel like this article pitches this as either-or: join the Lean fan-club and formalize everything all the time, or stay away from this at a distance. Can the two modes coexist, join forces, learn from each other, build each other up? Do they need each other?

I think the article even gives many examples where the answer is "yes". I wish it would also be the tone/conclusion.

It’s partly the article but it is also the mathematicians they quote who seem to consider formalisation an either-or issue. I can imagine that formalisation will have its counter reaction like any other new technology. This article seems to voice it. Also I don’t see why graph theory and combinatorics get picked out as places where formalisation is somehow bad. If anything that’s where formalization seems most useful for research level uses of AI

Johan Commelin said:

I feel like this article pitches this as either-or: join the Lean fan-club and formalize everything all the time, or stay away from this at a distance. Can the two modes coexist, join forces, learn from each other, build each other up? Do they need each other?

I think the article even gives many examples where the answer is "yes". I wish it would also be the tone/conclusion.

Funny, I didn't get that sense from reading the article. Like a lot of Quanta articles, it reports the views of a variety of mathematicians, without drawing a conclusion about who's "right."

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Also I don’t see why graph theory and combinatorics get picked out as places where formalisation is somehow bad. If anything that’s where formalization seems most useful for research level uses of AI

I was a little surprised by that, too, but earlier, the article says that combinatorics and graph theory are "concrete and visual," which I guess is somewhat in tension with "abstract and formal." Of course, it's not as simple as that, but it is true that highly computational proofs are awkward in Lean.

I actually found overly visual presentations of graph theory annoying as a first-time learner (way back in undergrad), because it was hard to make sense of what argument was valid or invalid in purely visual terms. Concretely I could never be sure if an argument I created was valid in general or whether my underdeveloped visualisation was misleading me. I am sure it is useful to think visually with graphs, but only as long as one can ground these arguments formally.

I have cited Jaffe and Quinn's Theoretical Mathematics before but can't resist citing it again, as well as Thurston's response, On proof and progress in mathematics. People often complained that Thurston's proofs were sketchy or incomplete or suspiciously visual. Thurston was somewhat sympathetic to the concerns, citing his own experience when first starting out, but also denied that his proofs weren't "really proofs."

I am not questioning the validity of visual proofs as proofs. I am just saying it is useful to have some way to check that I myself am not writing total nonsense. Even without lean this means I would like to prove things from rigorous definitions and at a reasonable level of rigour (which at my present stage is not a lot really). If anything formal proofs give those who don't share similar visualisation style to communicate their thinking in more neutral grounds checked by a theorem prover
7 messages were moved here from #general > Lean in the wild by Johan Commelin.

Johan Commelin said:

Can the two modes coexist, join forces, learn from each other, build each other up? Do they need each other?

My personal imagination is that in an ideal world, the relationship between informal and formal maths would look somewhat like that of theoretical and experimental physics. (I know it's not a perfect analogy, but it's the closest one I can think of.)
Which of the two sides is experimental, and which one is theoretical? :wink: :wink:

Johan Commelin said:

Which of the two sides is experimental, and which one is theoretical? :wink: :wink:

This is exactly the analogy that Jaffe and Quinn were making in their article. Experimental physics corresponds to formal verification.
The point of my :wink: :wink: is that you might as well argue that formal maths is the theoretical side, whereas the informal intuitive maths is the experimental side.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

I am not questioning the validity of visual proofs as proofs. I am just saying it is useful to have some way to check that I myself am not writing total nonsense. Even without lean this means I would like to prove things from rigorous definitions and at a reasonable level of rigour (which at my present stage is not a lot really). If anything formal proofs give those who don't share similar visualisation style to communicate their thinking in more neutral grounds checked by a theorem prover

Right, this is consistent with Thurston's point of view. Being supportive of formal proof does not automatically mean that you're opposed to less formal modes of thinking about, and communicating, mathematics.

But I think the Quanta article is right to point out that some mathematicians perceive a tension. You yourself referred to "overly visual" presentations that were "annoying," and some might perceive that to be a criticism of the informal approach.

Johan Commelin said:

The point of my :wink: :wink: is that you might as well argue that formal maths is the theoretical side, whereas the informal intuitive maths is the experimental side.

Ah, I see. I can see how someone might try to argue this, but the culture of modern experimental physics is very much that it's about verification and rock-solid facts. Observational science is perhaps a better analogy to informal, intuitive mathematics.

To clarify, the article said Graph theory and Combinatorics are examples of where too much Bourbaki-style abstraction is not suitable (and the formalization was viewed as somehow analogous to this, which is rather dubious). Gowers famous "two cultures" article is related to this.

Siddhartha Gadgil said:

To clarify, the article said Graph theory and Combinatorics are examples of where too much Bourbaki-style abstraction is not suitable (and the formalization was viewed as somehow analogous to this, which is rather dubious). Gowers famous "two cultures" article is related to this.

But the article also says this:

Just as Bourbaki’s approach was optimal for certain subjects and not others, the Lean language and the choice of definitions that go into its library are better suited to some areas of math than others. They’re a good fit for number theory and algebraic geometry, for instance. Graph theory and category theory, not so much.
Good point. The last part I also agree is plain wrong and based on carrying an analogy too far.
If graph theory in Lean is undeveloped it's only because it's one of the newer developments. I think time will inevitably gives us good abstractions we can settle on.
